questions.q: What is the main risk of right-sizing a VM based on its average CPU utilization over a month?
options: Average utilization cannot be queried from Azure Monitor or CloudWatch at all
A bursty workload — idle most of the day, pegged during a nightly batch job — can average out to a low number that hides the real peak
Averages are always higher than the real peak, so you'd oversize instead of undersize
Average utilization only applies to memory, never to CPU
questions.explain: A workload idle 23 hours and pegged for 1 hour can still average around 12% CPU; sizing off that average risks the batch job missing its window or falling over.

questions.q: Why do right-sizing workflows typically use p95 utilization instead of the mean?
options: p95 reflects real peak usage without letting one rare outlier dictate the whole sizing decision
p95 is simply another name for the average and the two numbers are interchangeable
p95 is only available in CloudWatch, never in Azure Monitor
p95 always equals the maximum observed value, so it's the safest possible number to use
questions.explain: p95 means utilization is below that value 95% of the time — it captures real peaks while being more stable than the raw max, unlike the mean which hides bursty load shapes entirely.

questions.q: In the Log Analytics KQL example in this lesson, what does `summarize p95 = percentile(CounterValue, 95) by Computer` actually produce?
options: A single p95 value across the entire subscription with no per-machine breakdown
The percentage of machines currently above 95% CPU
The 95th-percentile value of the CounterValue column, computed separately for each Computer
A list of every raw CounterValue reading, sorted from lowest to highest
questions.explain: The `by Computer` clause groups the percentile calculation per machine, giving a p95 CPU value for each VM over the queried window.

questions.q: A VM shows p95 CPU around 18% but p95 memory around 85% over a full month. What does this lesson say to do?
options: Resize the whole instance down uniformly, since CPU is the lower number
Ignore memory entirely — CPU is the only metric that matters for right-sizing
Delete the VM, since mismatched CPU and memory usage always indicates a misconfigured resource
Look for a SKU family with a different vCPU-to-memory ratio instead of resizing both dimensions the same way
questions.explain: When CPU and memory utilization point in different directions, a uniform resize either wastes CPU or starves memory — the fix is a SKU with a different ratio of the two.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend treating right-sizing as a recurring monthly or quarterly review rather than a one-time cleanup?
options: Azure Monitor and CloudWatch automatically delete utilization history after 30 days
Percentile queries only work correctly the first time they are run
New workloads tend to get provisioned generously again over time, so sizing drifts back upward unless it's re-checked on a cadence
Cloud providers change VM SKU pricing every month, making old right-sizing decisions invalid
questions.explain: A one-time right-sizing pass decays the same way the original drift happened — without a recurring review, new resources get provisioned generously again and the waste comes back.
